playbooks.title: Migrate key establishment to ML-KEM (hybrid first)
playbooks.appliesTo: Anything that establishes a shared secret over a channel: RSA key transport/encryption, ECDH, and finite-field Diffie-Hellman. This is the highest-urgency class because of harvest-now-decrypt-later: an adversary can record ciphertext today and decrypt it once a quantum computer exists, so the data's required confidentiality lifetime — not the migration deadline — is the real clock.
playbooks.target: Hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 during the transition; pure ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203, NIST security level 3 / CNSA 2.0) once every peer supports it.

approaches.name: Transport security (TLS) — often no application code change
approaches.status: Best first move for HTTPS/gRPC/database TLS. .NET 10 on a PQC-capable OS negotiates the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 by default; the secret is protected the moment both ends support it.
approaches.recommendedFor: Crypto that is really just 'TLS to another service.' Confirm the finding is transport, not application-layer key wrapping, before assuming you are done.
approaches.code:
1. Upgrade the service to .NET 10+.
2. Ensure the OS provides PQC primitives: OpenSSL 3.5+ (Linux/macOS) or Windows 11 / Server 2025 with PQC support.
3. Verify negotiation: the TLS key share should be X25519MLKEM768. No application code change is typically required.
approaches.caveats: A middlebox, load balancer, or peer that does not understand the hybrid group will fall back to classical X25519 — confirm end-to-end, and remember TLS protects data in transit only, not the harvest-now risk of data you key and store yourself.

approaches.name: In-box .NET 10 (System.Security.Cryptography.MLKem)
approaches.status: Recommended for application-layer key establishment on .NET 10+. The MLKem type is stable (no longer [Experimental]). Requires OpenSSL 3.5+ (Linux/macOS) or Windows 11 / Server 2025 with PQC; always gate on MLKem.IsSupported.
approaches.recommendedFor: Code that wraps/encrypts data keys yourself (envelope encryption, message encryption, key transport) rather than relying on TLS.
approaches.caveats: ML-KEM keys and ciphertexts are far larger than ECDH (encapsulation key ~1184 bytes, ciphertext ~1088 bytes for MLKem768) — budget for storage, MTU, and message size. The KEM only transports a secret; you still need a KDF + AEAD for the actual data.

approaches.name: Hybrid (X25519 + ML-KEM) for the transition
approaches.status: Safest interim posture: derive one key from BOTH an X25519 exchange and an ML-KEM encapsulation, then KDF the concatenation. The result stays secure if either primitive is later broken.
approaches.recommendedFor: Any system that must remain secure today against classical attackers and tomorrow against quantum ones, while PQC library/peer support is still maturing.
approaches.caveats: Bind a version/context label into the KDF info so the scheme can evolve. Never XOR the secrets — concatenate and KDF.

approaches.name: BouncyCastle (pre-.NET 10 or unsupported OS)
approaches.status: Use when you cannot run .NET 10 or a PQC-capable OS. The BouncyCastle.Cryptography package (>= 2.5.0) implements ML-KEM under Org.BouncyCastle.Pqc.Crypto.MLKem.
approaches.recommendedFor: Apps pinned to .NET 8/older runtimes or platforms without OpenSSL 3.5 / CNG PQC.
approaches.code: Add the BouncyCastle.Cryptography package (>= 2.5.0), then: generate a keypair with MLKemKeyPairGenerator (init with MLKemKeyGenerationParameters + MLKemParameters.ml_kem_768); on the sender side use MLKemEncapsulator (Init with the recipient's public key, then Encapsulate to get the ciphertext + shared secret); on the recipient side use MLKemDecapsulator (Init with the private key, then Decapsulate). Then derive a key with HKDF and encrypt with an AEAD, exactly as in the in-box example. Consult the current BouncyCastle .NET docs for the exact namespaces/imports in your package version.
approaches.caveats: Requires BouncyCastle.Cryptography >= 2.5.0, which replaced the pre-standard Kyber types with FIPS 203 ML-KEM. Treat as a transition bridge and move to the in-box API on .NET 10+, which uses the platform's validated crypto. Pin and review the dependency like any crypto library.

steps: Inventory every call site this rule flagged and classify each as transport (TLS) vs. application-layer key establishment — they have very different fixes.
Put the data's required confidentiality lifetime on each one. Long-lived secrets (records, backups, keys, health/financial/PII data) are the harvest-now-decrypt-later priorities; migrate them first.
Abstract key establishment behind an interface if it is currently inlined, so the algorithm can change without touching call sites (crypto agility).
Pilot the hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 approach in one low-risk service; measure key/ciphertext size and latency impact.
Roll out hybrid broadly; keep classical as the fallback until all peers negotiate PQC.
Re-scan with dotnet-cbom and confirm the finding moves to PostQuantum; record the change against your baseline.

playbooks.title: Migrate digital signatures to ML-DSA (or SLH-DSA)
playbooks.appliesTo: RSA, ECDSA, and DSA used for signing/verification: tokens (JWT), document/message signing, code/firmware signing, and certificate chains. Signatures are lower harvest-now urgency than key establishment — a signature forged after quantum arrives cannot retroactively forge yesterday's — but anything that must verify for years (firmware, long-lived roots, archived documents) needs a quantum-safe scheme now.
playbooks.target: ML-DSA (FIPS 204, NIST level 3 / CNSA 2.0) for general signatures; SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for long-lived or firmware/code signing where conservative hash-based security is worth the larger signatures.

approaches.name: In-box .NET 10 (System.Security.Cryptography.MLDsa)
approaches.status: Recommended on .NET 10+. The MLDsa type is stable (no longer [Experimental]; a few methods remain experimental). Requires OpenSSL 3.5+ (Linux/macOS) or Windows 11 / Server 2025 with PQC; gate on MLDsa.IsSupported.
approaches.recommendedFor: General-purpose signing and verification in services already on .NET 10.
approaches.caveats: ML-DSA signatures and keys are much larger than ECDSA (MLDsa65 signature ~3309 bytes, public key ~1952 bytes). Check token/header size limits (e.g. JWT in a cookie or HTTP header) before adopting.

approaches.name: SLH-DSA for firmware / code signing / long-lived roots
approaches.status: Stateless hash-based signatures (FIPS 205, SlhDsa type). Security rests only on the hash function, making it the conservative choice for things that must verify for a decade or more.
approaches.recommendedFor: Firmware/code signing, certificate roots, and archived-document signatures where longevity matters more than signature size.
approaches.caveats: SLH-DSA signatures are large (tens of KB depending on parameter set). Excellent for infrequent, high-assurance signing; poor for high-volume per-request signing.

approaches.name: Hybrid / composite signatures for certificates
approaches.status: .NET 10 adds CompositeMLDsa for X.509 scenarios that must carry both a classical and a PQC signature during transition (e.g. a CA that not-yet-PQC clients and PQC clients both trust).
approaches.recommendedFor: PKI and certificate chains migrating while a mixed population of relying parties exists.
approaches.code: Use CompositeMLDsa (System.Security.Cryptography) to produce a certificate signature that combines a traditional algorithm with ML-DSA, so both legacy and PQC-aware verifiers can validate during the transition.
approaches.caveats: Composite certificates are larger and require relying-party support; treat as a transition mechanism, not the end state.

approaches.name: BouncyCastle (pre-.NET 10 or unsupported OS)
approaches.status: Use when you cannot run .NET 10 / a PQC-capable OS. BouncyCastle.Cryptography (>= 2.5.0) implements ML-DSA under Org.BouncyCastle.Pqc.Crypto.MLDsa (and SLH-DSA).
approaches.recommendedFor: Apps pinned to older runtimes or platforms without OpenSSL 3.5 / CNG PQC.
approaches.code: Add the BouncyCastle.Cryptography package (>= 2.5.0), then: generate a keypair with MLDsaKeyPairGenerator (init with MLDsaKeyGenerationParameters + MLDsaParameters.ml_dsa_65); sign with MLDsaSigner (construct with the parameter set, Init(true, privateKey), BlockUpdate(data), GenerateSignature()); verify with another MLDsaSigner (Init(false, publicKey), BlockUpdate(data), VerifySignature(signature)). Consult the current BouncyCastle .NET docs for the exact namespaces/imports in your package version.
approaches.caveats: Requires BouncyCastle.Cryptography >= 2.5.0, which replaced the pre-standard Dilithium types with FIPS 204 ML-DSA. Treat as a bridge; move to the in-box API on .NET 10+. Pin and review like any crypto dependency.

steps: List every signing/verification call site this rule flagged and tag its purpose: token, document, message, or code/firmware signing.
Sort by verification lifetime. Firmware, certificate roots, and archived documents that must verify for years are the first to need a quantum-safe scheme; short-lived access tokens are lower urgency.
Check size budgets early — PQC signatures and keys are much larger; verify they fit your tokens, headers, certificates, and storage.
Abstract signing behind an interface so the algorithm is swappable without touching every call site.
Pilot ML-DSA (or SLH-DSA for long-lived signing) in one path; verify interop with every component that checks the signature.
Roll out, then re-scan with dotnet-cbom and confirm the finding moves to PostQuantum against your baseline.
